cards.b:
Evolution is supported by independent lines of evidence from rocks, bones, genes and living animals. When different methods point to the same story, confidence is very high. This lesson shows the main lines.

Think of a detective case where fingerprints, CCTV, phone records and witnesses all point to the same person. In evolution the 'witnesses' are fossils, anatomy, embryos, DNA, geography and direct observation. Each was studied by different scientists, often by people with no wish to support Darwin, yet they agree on the tree of life. A claim that explains all of them at once is very strong.

Fossils are preserved remains or traces. Deeper rock is older. Radiometric dating, using the steady decay of atoms like uranium and carbon-14, gives ages in years. Earth is about 4.54 billion years old; the earliest life dates to roughly 3.5 billion years ago.

Radiometric dating works like an hourglass: an unstable atom decays at a fixed rate, its half-life, so the ratio of parent to product tells the age. Carbon-14 (half-life about 5,730 years) dates remains up to about 50,000 years old, while uranium-lead dates rocks of millions to billions of years. Fossils in younger layers resemble modern life, and the oldest layers show simpler forms, in a pattern that never appears out of order. Claire Patterson fixed Earth's age in 1956 using lead in meteorites.

• Archaeopteryx (1861): feathers plus reptile teeth and tail.
  • Tiktaalik (2006): fish with a neck and wrist-like fins, about 375 million years old.
  • Whale ancestors: Pakicetus, found in Pakistan, and Rodhocetus show legs shrinking.

Transitional fossils show mixtures of traits, just as evolution predicts. Archaeopteryx lived about 150 million years ago, and many feathered dinosaurs have since been found in China. Neil Shubin and colleagues found Tiktaalik on Ellesmere Island in Canada after predicting which age of rock would hold such a fish. In India, Kutch and Himachal fossils, including Indohyus, a small deer-like relative of whales, helped trace the story of whales from land animals.

Homologous: same plan, different use. The human arm, whale flipper, bat wing and horse leg share the same bones, showing common ancestry. Analogous: same use, different origin: bird and insect wings. This is convergent evolution.

Human tailbone, appendix and ear muscles are leftovers. Whales have tiny hip bones. Embryos of fish, bird and human all show gill-like pouches early on, reflecting shared ancestry (Haeckel's old 'recapitulation' idea was overstated).

Vestigial structures are reduced parts that once served a larger function in ancestors, like the unused room of an old house. The human appendix may still serve a small immune role, so 'useless' is not always true. Embryos reveal that bodies are built by modifying older plans: all vertebrate embryos have a tail and pharyngeal arches, which become jaw and ear parts in humans. Karl von Baer noted these similarities in the 1820s, before Darwin.

All life uses DNA and nearly the same genetic code. The more recently two species split, the more alike their DNA and proteins. Humans and chimpanzees share about 98-99 percent of DNA sequence in aligned regions. Cytochrome c, a protein, is similar across species.

DNA is a record that can be read like a manuscript copied by scribes: shared mistakes show a shared source. Humans, chimps and gorillas share broken versions of the same vitamin C gene, which we cannot use, while most other mammals make their own vitamin C. We also share many 'viral fossil' insertions in the same places in our genomes. Together these give a family tree built from molecules that matches the one built from bones.

Bacteria become antibiotic resistant. Richard Lenski's E. coli experiment, running since 1988, has seen new traits arise over tens of thousands of generations. Insects evolve pesticide resistance.

Lenski's experiment started with twelve identical flasks of bacteria. One line learned to feed on citrate, which the starting bacteria could not use, after about 31,500 generations, a new ability that arose by a chain of mutations. Antibiotic resistance, such as multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, shows the same process in hospitals. Also, mosquitoes have evolved resistance to DDT, and Galapagos finch beaks changed within years of a drought, as measured by Peter and Rosemary Grant.

Wallace and Darwin noted that island species resemble nearby mainland ones, and that marsupials cluster in Australia. Plate tectonics (Wegener 1912; accepted 1960s) explains why related fossils like Glossopteris appear across southern continents.

Islands are natural laboratories: the finches, tortoises and mockingbirds of the Galapagos differ from island to island but resemble the South American mainland. Alfred Wallace drew a line between Asia and Australia where animal groups change abruptly. India's own story fits too: it drifted north as an island, from about 120 million years ago, and joined Asia about 50 million years ago, raising the Himalaya.

Fix these

  • Humans did not evolve from chimpanzees; we share a common ancestor.
  • 'Missing link' is not needed; many transitional fossils exist.
  • Evolution is observed, not only a past event.

Also, 'only a theory' misunderstands science: evolution is both a fact (populations change) and a theory (natural selection and other mechanisms explain how). Fossils are never expected to be complete, since only a tiny fraction of organisms become fossils, so gaps do not weaken the evidence.

Birbal Sahni (1891-1949) was India's pioneer of palaeobotany. He studied Gondwana fossil plants, and founded the Birbal Sahni Institute of Palaeosciences in Lucknow (1946, formally 1949). Shivalik hills in the north gave Ramapithecus and Sivapithecus ape fossils. Fossil whales like Indohyus from Kashmir, about 48 million years old, link whales to even-toed ungulates. Balasinor in Gujarat is a well-known dinosaur egg and fossil site.

• Fossils, comparative anatomy, embryos, molecules and observation agree.
  • Homologous means common ancestry; analogous means convergence.
  • Dating shows Earth is about 4.5 billion years old.

Think about it:

  1. Why are bird and bat wings analogous in some ways but homologous in others?
  2. What would disprove common ancestry?
